Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 56, verses 1–3:

(p-٥٦٤٤) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Waqi'ah (The Inevitable)

It is so named because it is filled with the events of the Resurrection, which are the Great Event (al-waqi'ah al-'uzma), for it occurs in the most intense of circumstances. Said by al-Mahayimi.

It is Meccan, and its verses number ninety-six.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you have grown gray!' He said: 'Hud, al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, 'Amma yatasa'alun, and idha al-shams kuwwirat have made me gray.'" Related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: it is hasan gharib.

It is narrated from Jabir ibn Samurah that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray the prayers in a manner similar to your prayers that you pray today, but he would make them lighter. His prayer was lighter than your prayer.

And he would recite in the Fajr prayer al-Waqi'ah and similar surahs."

(p-٥٦٤٥) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discourse on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[1–3] ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾ ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ ﴿it will bring low and it will raise high﴾

﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾ meaning: it descends and comes. "Al-waqi'ah" is a term that has become dominant for the Resurrection, or it is a derived term; it was named so for the certainty of its occurrence, as if it were said: when that occurs which must necessarily occur. The choice of "idha" with the past form is to indicate what has been mentioned.

﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ meaning: there is no lying and no denial. The verbal noun has come in the pattern fa'ilah like al-'aqibah and al-'afiyah. The lam is for specification. Or the meaning is: there will be no soul at the time of its occurrence that is lying, i.e., that lies about Allah, or lies in denying it. The lam is for time.

Al-Shihab said: "Al-waqi'ah" is a strong fall, and it has become common for the occurrence of a great matter, and it may be specific to war, and therefore it is expressed by it here.

﴿it will bring low and it will raise high﴾ meaning: it will bring the wretched down to the lowest levels, and raise the happy up to the high ranks. It has been said: the sentence confirms the greatness of the Event by way of metonymy, because it is characteristic of great events that they bring some people low and raise others high.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[4–6] ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ ﴿and the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5] ﴿and become scattered dust particles﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 6]

﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ means: it is quaked with a severe quaking.

(p-5646) ﴿And the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5] means: they are broken into fragments, or they are driven along and removed, like His words: ﴿and the mountains are set in motion﴾ [an-Naba': 20]. ﴿And become scattered dust particles﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 6] means: dispersed. Qatadah said: al-haba' (dust particles) is what the wind scatters of the debris of trees. Others said: it is what is seen in a sunbeam through a window, like the appearance of dust.

**The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying:**

[7–12] ﴿And you will be three kinds﴾ ﴿So the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 8] ﴿And the companions of the left hand — what are the companions of the left hand!﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 9] ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10] ﴿Those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11] ﴿In Gardens of Delight﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 12]

﴿وكُنْتُمْ أزْواجًا﴾ means: categories, three of them.

﴿فَأصْحابُ المَيْمَنَةِ ما أصْحابُ المَيْمَنَةِ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 8] ﴿وأصْحابُ المَشْأمَةِ ما أصْحابُ المَشْأمَةِ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 9] is a division and classification of the three pairs, with a general indication of their states before they are detailed. The terms "al-maymanah" (the right side, the place of the felicitous) and "al-mash'amah" (the left side, the place of the wretched) are two known directions. The first refers to the rank of the happy, who are the righteous and the reformers among people, and the second to the lowest rank of the wretched, who are the wicked and the corrupters among people. Its origin lies in the Arabs' taking the right hand as auspicious and the left as inauspicious, as in (the omens) "al-sani'" (a sign passing from left to right, deemed auspicious) and "al-barih" (a sign passing from right to left, deemed inauspicious), and in their saying of the exalted person, "He is from me on the right," and of the lowly, "He is from me on the left." This is used figuratively, or as a metonymy for what has been mentioned.

It is also said that "al-maymanah" and "al-mash'amah" mean "blessing" and "misfortune" respectively, and so they do not mean a direction; rather, they mean blessing and its opposite, due to what returns upon them from their own selves and their deeds. In the two interrogative clauses there is an indication of the ascending progression of their states in good and in evil, expressing amazement at it.

﴿والسّابِقُونَ السّابِقُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10] means: those who hastened to faith and obedience after the truth became manifest, who were harmed for its sake, who endured what befell them, and who were its callers.

If it is asked: why were those mentioned as "the foremost" differed from the companions of the right hand, although each of them is mentioned only to magnify and emphasise the state of those mentioned?

We say: the magnification conveyed by His saying ﴿السّابِقُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10] is more emphatic than its counterpart, because what this conveys is that the matter of the foremost and the greatness of their station is one that is already known (lit. "preceded"), which is almost hidden. The listener's confusion regarding it is well known. As for what is mentioned in His saying ﴿فَأصْحابُ المَيْمَنَةِ ما أصْحابُ المَيْمَنَةِ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 8], it is a magnification imposed upon the listener with something he has no prior knowledge of. Do you not see how the description of the foremost was preceded by His saying ﴿أُولَئِكَ المُقَرَّبُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11], so that He combined the demonstrative noun referring to something known, and clarified the predicate about it with His saying "al-muqarrabun" (the ones brought near), defined by the definite article of prior reference (al-'ahdiyyah)? Nothing like this is mentioned in the description of the companions of the right hand, since it begins with His saying ﴿فِي سِدْرٍ مَخْضُودٍ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28]. This was stated by al-Nasir.

The second ﴿السّابِقُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10] is either a predicate, meaning: those whose state is known and whose attributes are famous, in the manner of the idiom "wa shi'ri shi'ri" (lit. "and my poetry, my poetry," an expression of the speaker's self-assertion of the familiar); or it is an emphatic repetition, with the predicate being His saying ﴿أُولَئِكَ المُقَرَّبُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11], meaning: those whom God brings near to Himself by elevating their ranks ﴿فِي جَنّاتِ النَّعِيمِ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 12]. (p-5647)

﴿وكُنْتُمْ أزْواجًا﴾ means: categories, three of them.

The terms "al-maymanah" (the right side, the place of the felicitous) and "al-mash'amah" (the left side, the place of the wretched) are two known directions. The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[13–14] ﴿A multitude of the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a few of the later peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 13–14]

﴿A multitude of the earlier peoples﴾ means: they are a large group of those who went before, due to the firmness of their faith and the manifestation of its effect in their deeds, from righteous action, calling to Allah, patience in striving (jihad) in His cause, and other virtues that had become settled dispositions in them.

﴿And a few of the later peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 14] means: those who came after them, in the times when innovations (ghiyar) appeared, the world displayed its adornments to its suitors, and along with that the secret of the mission (al-ba'thah) and the wisdom of the call (al-da'wah) were forgotten. How few are those who walk in the footsteps of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions! Without doubt, at that time they are the strangers (al-ghuraba'), because of their scarcity.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[15–26] ﴿Upon thrones woven together﴾ ﴿reclining upon them, facing one another﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 16] ﴿There will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17] ﴿with cups, and jugs, and a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18] ﴿They will not be affected with headache by it, nor will they be intoxicated﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19] ﴿and fruit of what they select﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 20] ﴿and the flesh of fowl of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 21] ﴿and wide-eyed maidens﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22] ﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 23] ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24] ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25] ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26]

﴿Upon thrones woven together﴾: that is, arranged in rows, or interlaced with pearls, rubies, or gold. And (al-Waḍn) (p-5649) means interlacing and weaving.

﴿reclining upon them, facing one another﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 16]: that is, face to face, equal in rank, with no barrier between them at all.

﴿There will circulate among them﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: that is, to serve them. ﴿young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: that is, kept at one age, never dying.

﴿with cups, and jugs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: that is, at the time of drinking. The kūb (cup) is a vessel with no handle and no spout, and the ibrīq (jug) is a vessel that has these.

﴿and a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: that is, wine flowing freely.

Then He indicated that it is entirely pleasure, with no pain or intoxication accompanying it: ﴿They will not be affected with headache by it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19], that is, their heads will not ache because of intoxicant, as with the wines of this world. Ṣudāʿ (headache) is pain of the head. It was also read with shaddah as a tafaʿʿul form, meaning they will not scatter. ﴿nor will they be intoxicated﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19], with the zāy vowelled both with kasrah and with fatḥah; that is, their minds will not be taken away by its intoxication.

﴿and fruit of what they select﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 20]: that is, they choose and approve, and its root is taking the best and the good.

Ibn Kathir said: This verse is evidence for the permissibility of eating fruit in the manner of selecting from it. He then cited as support the ḥadīth of ʿIkrāsh: "When the Prophet ﷺ was brought a thārīd, and ʿIkrāsh came and began reaching with his hand into its sides, the Prophet ﷺ seized his hand and said: 'O ʿIkrāsh! Eat from one place, for it is one kind of food.' Then a tray containing dates or fresh dates was brought, and ʿIkrāsh began eating from in front of himself, and the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ moved around the tray, and he said: 'O ʿIkrāsh! Eat from wherever you wish, for it is not one colour.'" Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who considered it gharīb.

﴿and the flesh of fowl of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 21]: that is, what they wish for. ﴿and wide-eyed maidens﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22]: that is, and spouses, white, large-eyed. It is either coordinated with "young boys" or is a subject with an omitted predicate, meaning: and therein; or: and for them are maidens. It was also read in the genitive, coordinated with ﴿cups﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]. Al-Shihab said: In that case, either it is said that "yaṭūf" is used in the sense of "they are made to enjoy" figuratively or metonymically, after the manner of his saying:

"And they made the eyebrows and the eyes beautiful"

(p-5650) Or it remains in its literal sense, and its apparent meaning is that the young boys also circulate among them with the maidens, to present to them kinds of pleasures, of food, drink and intercourse, just as servants bring concubines to kings and present them to them. This was the view of Abu ʿAmr and Qutrub, and it was permitted to make it a genitive by jiwār (adjacency). It has been said: the separation (of the phrase) rejects this and weakens it. As for coordinating it with "gardens" by supposing an omitted noun, meaning: they are in gardens and in the company of maidens, Abu Hayyan said: this is a non-Arab understanding, with distance and a breaking apart of the connected speech, and it is clear. Whoever fanatically defends it has been fanatical.

﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 23]: that is, their clarity is like the clarity of pearls in the shells which no hand touches. The root of ﴿hidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 23] is that which is protected in a covering.

﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24]: that is, of righteous deeds.

﴿They will not hear therein﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25] ﴿any idle talk﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: that is, raving and speech with no benefit, vain talk.

﴿or sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: that is, what constitutes sin, such as obscenity, lying, backbiting and the like.

﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26]: al-Qashani said: that is, a saying which is itself peace, free from defects, cleansed of excess and superfluity; or a saying which conveys to the listener safety from faults and defects, and brings about his joy and honour, and manifests his perfection and delight, because all their speech is knowledge and realities, greetings and subtleties. This is according to the two grammatical possibilities, namely whether "salāman" is a substitute for "qīlan" or its object. The repetition is to indicate the spreading of greeting among them and its abundance, because the meaning is: peace after peace, like "I read grammar chapter by chapter," so it indicates its repetition and abundance.

﴿There will circulate among them﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: that is, to serve them. ﴿young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: that is, kept at one age, never dying.

﴿with cups, and jugs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: that is, at the time of drinking. The kūb (cup) is a vessel with no handle and no spout, and the ibrīq (jug) is a vessel that has these.

﴿and a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: that is, wine flowing freely.

Then He indicated that it is entirely pleasure, with no pain or intoxication accompanying it: ﴿They will not be affected with headache by it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19], that is, their heads will not ache because of intoxicant, as with the wines of this world. Ṣudāʿ (headache) is pain of the head. It was also read with shaddah as a tafaʿʿul form, meaning they will not scatter. ﴿nor will they be intoxicated﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19], with the zāy vowelled both with kasrah and with fatḥah; that is, their minds will not be taken away by its intoxication.

﴿and fruit of what they select﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 20]: that is, they choose and approve, and its root is taking the best and the good.

Ibn Kathir said: This verse is evidence for the permissibility of eating fruit in the manner of selecting from it. He then cited as support the ḥadīth of ʿIkrāsh: "When the Prophet ﷺ was brought a thārīd, and ʿIkrāsh came and began reaching with his hand into its sides, the Prophet ﷺ seized his hand and said: 'O ʿIkrāsh! Eat from one place, for it is one kind of food.' Then a tray containing dates or fresh dates was brought, and ʿIkrāsh began eating from in front of himself, and the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ moved around the tray, and he said: 'O ʿIkrāsh! Eat from wherever you wish, for it is not one colour.'" Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who considered it gharīb.

﴿and the flesh of fowl of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 21]: that is, what they wish for. ﴿and wide-eyed maidens﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22]: that is, and spouses, white, large-eyed. It is either coordinated with "young boys" or is a subject with an omitted predicate, meaning: and therein; or: and for them are maidens. It was also read in the genitive, coordinated with ﴿cups﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]. Al-Shihab said: In that case, either it is said that "yaṭūf" is used in the sense of "they are made to enjoy" figuratively or metonymically, after the manner of his saying:

"And they made the eyebrows and the eyes beautiful"

(p-5650) Or it remains in its literal sense, and its apparent meaning is that the young boys also circulate among them with the maidens, to present to them kinds of pleasures, of food, drink and intercourse, just as servants bring concubines to kings and present them to them. This was the view of Abu ʿAmr and Qutrub, and it was permitted to make it a genitive by jiwār (adjacency). It has been said: the separation (of the phrase) rejects this and weakens it. As for coordinating it with "gardens" by supposing an omitted noun, meaning: they are in gardens and in the company of maidens, Abu Hayyan said: this is a non-Arab understanding, with distance and a breaking apart of the connected speech, and it is clear. Whoever fanatically defends it has been fanatical.

﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 23]: that is, their clarity is like the clarity of pearls in the shells which no hand touches. The root of ﴿hidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 23] is that which is protected in a covering.

﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24]: that is, of righteous deeds.

﴿They will not hear therein﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25] ﴿any idle talk﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: that is, raving and speech with no benefit, vain talk.

﴿or sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: that is, what constitutes sin, such as obscenity, lying, backbiting and the like.

﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26]: al-Qashani said: that is, a saying which is itself peace, free from defects, cleansed of excess and superfluity; or a saying which conveys to the listener safety from faults and defects, and brings about his joy and honour, and manifests his perfection and delight, because all their speech is knowledge and realities, greetings and subtleties. This is according to the two grammatical possibilities, namely whether "salāman" is a substitute for "qīlan" or its object. The repetition is to indicate the spreading of greeting among them and its abundance, because the meaning is: peace after peace, like "I read grammar chapter by chapter," so it indicates its repetition and abundance.

﴿And the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ That is: what a state they are in! That is, they are noble, honored and generous, and their qualities of happiness are a matter of wonder.

﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ That is, having no thorns, or laden with fruit.

﴿And acacias arranged in tiers﴾ This means banana trees, whose fruit is arranged in clusters from their base to their top. Mujahid said: "They used to admire a wadi (valley) of their acacias and lote-trees." The fruit of the banana tree is sweet, rich and delicious, and has no seeds.

﴿And shade extended﴾ That is, spreading out, stretched, never contracting.

﴿And water poured out﴾ That is, flowing, constantly running.

﴿And fruit in abundance﴾ ﴿Neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ That is, it is not cut off from them whenever they desire it, because it is not limited. ﴿Nor forbidden﴾ That is, it is not withheld from the one who seeks it. The intent is to contrast it with the fruit of this world, which is sometimes cut off, like summer fruit in winter, and sometimes withheld because of its scarcity or dearth.

﴿And raised couches﴾ That is, elevated in their places, or on couches for reclining and lying together. This may be supported by the reference to those who lie with them (p-5652) in it, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾ That is, wondrous and of surpassing description. The pronoun refers to what is understood from the context (siyaq) and the preceding passage (sibaq). It has been said: the houris may be alluded to by "couches," just as they are alluded to by "clothing," so the pronoun here is in the manner of istikhdam (a rhetorical device in which a word is used in one sense and its pronoun in another), since it refers to "couches" in the sense of "women," after the commonly known meaning has been intended. It has also been said: it is meant literally, that is, raised upon couches, like His saying: ﴿They and their spouses, in shade, reclining on couches﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56].

﴿And We made them virgins﴾ That is, they have not been touched.

﴿Loving, of equal age﴾ "Uruban" is the plural of 'aroob, the one who is affectionate toward her husband, beloved for her devotion to him. ﴿Of equal age﴾ That is, of one age.

﴿For the companions of the right hand﴾ This is related to "We produced" or "We made," or it is an attribute of ﴿virgins﴾, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, like "they are."

﴿A multitude from the earlier generations﴾ ﴿And a multitude from the later generations﴾ That is, a group and a community from those who preceded in faith, and from those who came after them of the followers of them in goodness from this nation. The abundance is evident, given the great number of the companions of the right hand among the later ones compared with the foremost, as we explained at the beginning.

(p-5653) ﴿And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left?﴾ That is: a heat of fire that penetrates the pores pervading [the body].

﴿And boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 42], that is: water of extreme heat.

﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 43], that is: from black smoke, corresponding to their corrupt desires, their ruinous beliefs, and the blackened states of their souls, [marked] by dark attributes and evil, black conditions.

﴿Neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 44], that is: it has none of the two qualities of the shade to which people resort, [namely] refreshment, and benefit to the one who takes refuge in it with comfort; rather, it brings harm, pain and injury, by inflicting fatigue, flame and distress.

﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 45], that is: immersed in pleasures and desires, sunk in natural matters and bodily excesses; by this they acquired these destructive states and these ruinous consequences.

﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 46], that is: the great sin of false sayings and corrupt beliefs, by which they deserved everlasting punishment and perpetual chastisement. As-Subki interpreted it as swearing [oaths] to deny resurrection, referred to by the words of the Exalted:

﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die﴾ [an-Nahl: 38]. Al-Shihab said: This is a good interpretation, because al-Hinth (violation) — even if it is explained as sin in general or great sin — is known in usage as failing to fulfil an oath; therefore it is connected with what they believed of denying resurrection, by His saying:

﴿And they used to say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? Or our forefathers of old?"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 47–48]

Commentary on the Meaning of His Words, Exalted is He:

[57–62] ﴿We created you, so why do you not affirm the truth?﴾ ﴿Have you considered that which you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58] ﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59] (p-5655) ﴿We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60] ﴿in replacing your likes and producing you in what you do not know﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 61] ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not take heed?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62]

﴿We created you﴾ means: O assembly of Quraysh and those who deny the Resurrection, We brought you into existence as human beings when you were nothing. ﴿So why do you not affirm the truth?﴾ means: [affirm] the creation. Although they acknowledge it, given His words: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25], their acknowledgment was treated as though it were non-existent and as denial, because when it is not accompanied by obedience and righteous deeds, it is not counted as affirmation. Or the meaning is: why do you not affirm the Resurrection? For the One who is able to originate is able to restore.

﴿Have you considered that which you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58] means: that which you discharge into the womb of the drops of semen (nutfah).

﴿Is it you who create it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59] means: by making it a complete human being.

﴿Or are We the Creator?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59] means: by bestowing upon it the human form.

﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60] means: We have prescribed for every soul the tasting of it. That is, whoever is subject to that should fear its approach and prepare for what he is warned of after it. This sentence confirms what precedes it, indicating that they are within the grip of power, so they should not be deceived by the respite, as evidenced by the death He has decreed upon them. Regarding His words, Exalted is He, "among you," there is an added emphasis of warning, as if it were in their midst. Then He confirmed what He had established with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and We are not to be outdone﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60], meaning: not overcome.

﴿in replacing your likes﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 61] means: after your destruction, We will bring others of your kind. ﴿and producing you in what you do not know﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 61], of other forms and shapes. So how could We be incapable of restoring you?

Al-Shihab said: The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿and producing you﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 61], refer to when We replace you with others, not in the Hereafter, as has been thought. This is like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿If He wills, He will remove you, O people, and bring others﴾ [an-Nisa': 133]. ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62] means: that He originated you after you were not a thing worth mentioning, so He created you and made for you hearing, sight and hearts. ﴿So why do you not take heed?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62] means: so that you may recognise that the One who is able to bring about this first origination, which is the beginning, is able to bring about the other origination, which is the restoration, and that the latter is easier for Him.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 56, verses 63–67:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[63–67] ﴿Have you considered what you plant?﴾ ﴿Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 64] ﴿If We willed, We could make it into debris, and you would be left astonished﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65] ﴿"Indeed, we are laden with debt!"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66] ﴿"Rather, we are deprived!"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 67]

﴿Have you considered what you plant?﴾ That is: what you till the land for, which is the grain. And (al-harth, "tilling"): splitting the earth for cultivation, stirring it up, and casting the seed into it.

﴿Is it you who make it grow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 64] That is: do you cause it to sprout, ﴿or are We the growers?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 64] That is: the ones who cause it to sprout. It is reported from some of the early generations (al-salaf) that when he recited this verse and similar ones he would say: "Rather, You, O Lord!"

﴿If We willed, We could make it into debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65] That is: We could dry it up before it became ripe and ready for harvest. The root of (al-hutam, "debris") is that which is broken and crumbled due to its extreme dryness.

﴿And you would be left astonished﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65] That is: you would marvel at its ruin and dryness after its greenness. Or: you would regret your efforts in it, which were wasted and lost. Or: (tafakkahun) means you would boast of the sins you committed for its sake, and so you would talk about it. And (al-tafakkuh): moving among various kinds of fruit; it has been used metaphorically for moving from one topic of conversation to another, since it has many branches (dhu shujun).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Indeed, we are laden with debt!"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66] is the object of an implied saying, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: saying, or they will say, "Indeed, we are laden with debt!" That is: we are obligated to pay the cost of what we spent, or we are ruined by the loss of our provision. From (gharam) in the sense of ruin, he said:

"If He punishes, it will be a ruin; and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."

﴿"Rather, we are deprived!"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 67] That is: we have been deprived of our provision.

(p-5657)

**On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[68–70] ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink?﴾ ﴿Is it you who brought it down from the rain-cloud, or are We the ones who bring it down?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 69] ﴿If We willed, We could make it bitter; so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70]

﴿Have you considered the water which you drink?﴾ means: the sweet water fit for drinking.

﴿Is it you who brought it down from the rain-cloud﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 69], i.e., the clouds, which are referred to as "sky" in more than one verse, ﴿or are We the ones who bring it down?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 69], i.e., to you, to the bottom of the earth, and We make it flow into springs within it.

﴿If We willed, We could make it bitter﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], i.e., salt, unfit for drinking or for cultivation. ﴿so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], i.e., for God's blessing upon you in making it sweet and pleasant, for your drinking and your crops, and for the well-being of your livelihoods and your benefits.

**A subtle point (Latifah):**

The Imam Ibn al-Athir said in *al-Mathal al-Sa'ir*, in the eleventh type of the second treatise, in the discussion of the occurrence of the emphatic lam (lam al-tawkid) in speech, and that it only comes for a kind of emphasis, concerning the secret of the lam's occurrence in His saying, ﴿We could have made it crumbled debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65], instead of His saying, ﴿We could make it bitter﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70]. Its example is as follows:

The lam was introduced in the verse about food, but not in the verse about drink. It came in this way because making sweet water salty is easier to achieve by custom and habit, and salty water is more common than sweet water. Often, when sweet waters flow over lands whose soil has changed, they turn it salty. Therefore, making sweet water salty did not require additional emphasis, and so the emphatic lam, which conveys added certainty, was not attached to it. As for food, He made it crumbled debris, one of the things that lie outside the usual, and when it happens it can only be from a severe displeasure of God. Therefore it was joined with the emphatic lam, for added certainty regarding the matter and for affirming its occurrence. End of quote.

(p-٥٦٥٨)

The discussion of the words of the Exalted:

[71–74] ﴿Have you considered the fire which you ignite?﴾ ﴿Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producer?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 72] ﴿We made it a reminder and a provision for the travelers.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73] ﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74]

﴿Have you considered the fire which you ignite?﴾ That is, which you strike out, i.e., you extract it from the flint (zand), which is the stick from which fire is struck.

﴿Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producer?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 72] That is: rather, We placed it deposited in a place. The Arabs have two trees: one is the markh (marakh) and the other is the 'iffar. When two green branches are taken from them and one is rubbed against the other, sparks of fire fly out between them. Its explanation has already preceded at the end of Surat Ya-Sin.

﴿We made it a reminder﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73] That is: We made the fire of the flint an insight into the matter of resurrection, for whoever brings fire out of the green tree, which is its opposite, is capable of restoring what its components have scattered; or it is a reminder of the Fire of Hell. ﴿And a provision﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73], that is, a benefit, ﴿for the travelers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73], that is, the wayfarers who alight in the qiwa', which is the desert waste. It is said: aqwa when he alighted in the qiwa', as asḥara when he entered the open desert, for the form af'ala here denotes entering into the state of its root verb. It is reported from Mujahid: "al-muqwin" means those who benefit, both the traveler and the resident.

It is reported from Ibn Zayd: they are the hungry. The Arabs say: "aqwaytu minhu kadha wa-kadha," meaning: I ate nothing from it. And "aqwat al-dar" means: the house became empty of its inhabitants and of their benefit from it, because they used to cook in it. Because of their great need for it, they were singled out for mention, although others also benefit from it.

﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74] That is: glorify His name. al-Zamakhshari said: by saying "Subhan Allah," either as declaring Him free of what the wrongdoers say, who deny His oneness and disbelieve His favor, or as wonder at their conduct in disdaining His manifest blessings and bounties, or as thanks to God for the favors He enumerated and drew attention to.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[75–79] ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ (56:76) ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ (56:77) ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ (56:78) ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ (56:79).

﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾: that is, the stations and the bright locations of the stars in the sky. Or by their setting places and their sunsets, which are the times of their disappearance from the senses. Or by their falling and their scattering on the Day of Resurrection. The "lā" in "lā uqsimu" is either an extra particle for emphasis and for strengthening the speech, and its addition is well attested in their speech, as clarified in *Fiqh al-Lugha* (the Jurisprudence of Language). Or it is not extra, and "lā uqsimu" is in its entirety a form of oath, as preferred by some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqīn).

﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ (56:76): that is, because of what the oath contains of indication of great power and perfection of wisdom.

﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ (56:77): that is, it possesses nobility, honour and lofty standing, because it comprises the foundations of wisdom and rulings, and that which the needs of mankind are fitted to at all times.

﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ (56:78): that is, protected and preserved, neither changing nor being altered. Or protected from being handled by hands repeatedly, like other books; rather, it is like a preserved pearl, reserved only for its people, as He said: ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ (56:79).

Know that there are many opinions regarding the verse, all of which return to whether the "touching" (*mass*) is metaphorical (*majāz*) or literal (*ḥaqīqa*), whether the pronoun refers to the Book in the sense of the received revelation or to the codex (*muṣḥaf*), and whether ﴿the purified﴾ (56:79) are the angels or those who purify themselves from minor and major impurities (*aḥdāth* and *akhbāth*). This is because of the breadth of these two noble expressions, by way of homonymy (*ishtirāk*), or literal and metaphorical meaning, as mentioned. Here is the summary and essence of that:

[p. 5660] As for the majority of the exegetes (*mufassirūn*): they hold that the verse means the angels. Thus, the negation of touching it is a metaphor (*kināya*) for its necessary consequence, which is the negation of having access to it and to what is in it. In this case, "the purified" (*al-muṭahharīn*) means either the class of angels, or those who brought it down, namely the Holy Spirit (*rūḥ al-quds*). Their purity is the cleanness of their essences from the turbidity of bodies and the stain of matter (*hayūlā*), or from opposition and disobedience.

Ibn Zayd said: The disbelievers of Quraysh claimed that this Qur'an had been brought down by the devils, so God, exalted is He, informed that it is: ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ (56:79), as He said:

﴿And the devils did not bring it down﴾ (26:210) ﴿nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able to﴾ (26:211) ﴿Indeed, they are removed far from hearing it﴾ (26:212). End of quote. Ibn Kathir said: This opinion is a good opinion.

Al-Farrā' said: None finds its taste or its benefit except the one who believes in it. Similar is the statement of Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl: None recites it except the monotheists (*muwaḥḥidūn*).

Thus, the negation of touching it is a metaphor for not accepting it, not being guided by it, and not caring for it. For touching a thing is the cause of loving what is touched, the effect of turning towards it, and the guide to submitting to it. The purity in this case is the cleanness of the heart from the stain of polytheism (*shirk*) and hypocrisy (*nifāq*), the bad dispositions, and the corrupt natural inclinations.

Others said: By "the purified" (*al-muṭṭahharīn*) is meant those who purify themselves from major impurity (*janāba*) and minor impurity (*ḥadath*). They said: The wording of the verse is a statement (*khabar*), but its meaning is a prohibition, as an indication that this attribute is one of its natures and a necessary part of its features, due to its nobility and the greatness of its status.

They said: The "Book" means the codex (*muṣḥaf*), and they argued with what Imam Mālik narrated in his *Muwaṭṭa'* from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, that in the document which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote for ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm: "That none touches the Qur'an except one who is pure." And with what al-Dāraquṭnī narrated in the story of ʿUmar's conversion to Islam, that his sister said to him before he embraced Islam: "Indeed, it is filth, and ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ (56:79)." However, there is a critique in both of them [p. 5661] that al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar explained in *Talkhīṣ al-Ḥabīr*, and Ibn Kathir also alluded to it. Nevertheless, the indication is not decisive, and al-Shawkānī clarified this in *Nayl al-Awṭār*, and his words are:

"The word *ṭāhir* (pure) is applied by homonymy (*ishtirāk*) to the believer, to one free from major and minor impurity, and to one whose body has no impurity. What indicates its application to the first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The polytheists are only unclean﴾ (9:28), and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Abū Hurayra: 'The believer does not become impure.' As for the second: ﴿And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves﴾ (5:6). As for the third: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying regarding wiping over the leather socks: 'Leave them, for I put them on while they were pure.' As for the fourth: the consensus that a thing on which there is no physical or legal impurity is called pure. This usage is attested in many places. Whoever permits carrying a homonym on all its meanings, carries it on all of them here. The matter is recorded in the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl*), and there are positions on it; what is preponderant is that the homonym is ambiguous (*mujmal*) regarding its meanings, so it is not acted upon until it is clarified. The consensus is that it is not permissible for one in a major state of ritual impurity to touch the codex, and Dāwūd dissented in this. Those who prohibit touching for one in major impurity cite His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ (56:79), and this only holds after making the pronoun refer to the Qur'an, whereas the apparent reference is to the Book, which is the Preserved Tablet, because it is the nearest. And ﴿the purified﴾ are the angels. Even if one grants that it is not manifest, there is at least a possibility, so acting on either of the two matters is impossible, and the reference reverts to the original presumption of non-liability. Even if one grants that it refers to the Qur'an specifically, its indication for the sought ruling, namely the prohibition on the major-impure touching it, is not accepted; for the purified is one who is not unclean, and the believer is not always unclean, due to the ḥadīth: 'The believer does not become impure,' which is agreed upon. So it is not valid to interpret the purified as one who is not in major impurity, menstruation, minor impurity, or one whose body has a physical impurity; rather, it is determined that it be interpreted as one who is not a polytheist, as in His saying: ﴿The polytheists are only unclean﴾ (9:28), because of this ḥadīth, and because of the ḥadīth forbidding travel with the Qur'an to the enemy's land. Even if one grants the truth of the name *ṭāhir* for one who is not in major or minor ritual impurity, you have known that the preponderant view is that the homonym is ambiguous in its meanings, so it is not specified until it is made clear. The proof here indicates that what is meant is other than that, due to the ḥadīth: 'The believer does not become impure.' Even if one grants that there is no proof preventing its intended meaning, specifying it for the locus of dispute would be preferring without a preferrer, and specifying it for all of them would be using the homonym in all its meanings, and about that there is disagreement. Even if one grants the preponderance of the view permitting use in all its meanings, it would not be valid due to the presence of the impediment, which is the ḥadīth: 'The believer does not become impure.'

They also cited the ḥadīth of ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm mentioned earlier, and it was answered that it is not suitable for argument, because it is from a document not heard directly, and there is severe disagreement about the men in its chain. Even if one grants its suitability for argument, the earlier discussion of the word *ṭāhir* would return, and you have known it."

The Sayyid, the scholar Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Wazīr, said: The application of the name *najis* (impure) to a believer who is not pure from major impurity, menstruation, or minor impurity is not valid, either literally, metaphorically, or linguistically. He declared this in an answer to a question and refuted it. If this is established, then the believer is always pure, and so the ḥadīth does not encompass him, whether he is in major impurity, menstruation, minor impurity, or has a physical impurity on his body. If you say: If what you intend, namely interpreting *ṭāhir* as one who is not a polytheist, is complete, then what is your answer regarding what is established in the agreed-upon ḥadīth from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans: "Embrace Islam and you will be safe; embrace Islam and God will give you your reward twice. But if you turn away, then upon you is the sin of the Arisiyyin. And ﴿O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable﴾ (3:64) until His saying: ﴿Muslims﴾ (3:64)," while they combine both the impurity of polytheism and the state of being in need of purification, and their touching of it is known?

I say: I make this specific to a verse or two like it, for it is permissible to allow a polytheist to touch that amount for a benefit, such as calling him to Islam. It may be answered that by its mixing with other things (p-5663) its touching is not prohibited, like books of tafsir; so the verse and the ḥadīth are not specified by it. Having established this, you know that the evidence does not stand against preventing anyone other than the polytheist. You have known the disagreement regarding the one in major impurity. As for one in minor impurity: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Muʾayyad billāh, the Hādawiyya, the Chief Judge (Qāḍī al-Quḍāt) and Dāwūd held that it is permissible for him to touch the codex. Al-Qāsim, the majority of jurists, and Imam Yaḥyā said: It is not permissible. They cited what has preceded, and what is in it has preceded. End of al-Shawkānī's words.

**A note on the subtle indication of this verse and what it points to of hidden knowledge:**

If you say: If what you intend, namely interpreting *ṭāhir* as one who is not a polytheist, is complete, then what is your answer regarding what is established in the agreed-upon ḥadīth from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans: "Embrace Islam and you will be safe; embrace Islam and God will give you your reward twice. And ﴿O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable﴾ (3:64) until His saying: ﴿Muslims﴾ (3:64)," while they combine both the impurity of polytheism and the state of being in need of purification, and their touching of it is known?

Having established this, you know that the evidence does not stand against preventing anyone other than the polytheist. You have known the disagreement regarding the one in major impurity. As for one in minor impurity: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Muʾayyad billāh, the Hādawiyya, the Chief Judge (Qāḍī al-Quḍāt) and Dāwūd held that it is permissible for him to touch the codex. Even if one grants the truth of the name *ṭāhir* for one who is not in major or minor ritual impurity, you have known that the preponderant view is that the homonym is ambiguous in its meanings, so it is not specified until it is made clear. The proof here indicates that what is meant is other than that, due to the ḥadīth: 'The believer does not become impure.' Even if one grants that there is no proof preventing its intended meaning, specifying it for the locus of dispute would be preferring without a preferrer, and specifying it for all of them would be using the homonym in all its meanings, and about that there is disagreement. Even if one grants the preponderance of the view permitting use in all its meanings, it would not be valid due to the presence of the impediment, which is the ḥadīth: 'The believer does not become impure.'

They also cited the ḥadīth of ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm mentioned earlier, and it was answered that it is not suitable for argument, because it is from a document not heard directly, and there is severe disagreement about the men in its chain. Even if one grants its suitability for argument, the earlier discussion of the word *ṭāhir* would return, and you have known it."

The Sayyid, the scholar Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Wazīr, said: The application of the name *najis* (impure) to a believer who is not pure from major impurity, menstruation, or minor impurity is not valid, either literally, metaphorically, or linguistically. He declared this in an answer to a question and refuted it. If this is established, then the believer is always pure, and so the ḥadīth does not encompass him, whether he is in major impurity, menstruation, minor impurity, or has a physical impurity on his body. If you say: If what you intend, namely interpreting *ṭāhir* as one who is not a polytheist, is complete, then what is your answer regarding what is established in the agreed-upon ḥadīth from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans: "Embrace Islam and you will be safe; embrace Islam and God will give you your reward twice. But if you turn away, then upon you is the sin of the Arisiyyin. And ﴿O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable﴾ (3:64) until His saying: ﴿Muslims﴾ (3:64)," while they combine both the impurity of polytheism and the state of being in need of purification, and their touching of it is known?

I say: I make this specific to a verse or two like it, for it is permissible to allow a polytheist to touch that amount for a benefit, such as calling him to Islam. It may be answered that by its mixing with other things (p-5663) its touching is not prohibited, like books of tafsir; so the verse and the ḥadīth are not specified by it. Having established this, you know that the evidence does not stand against preventing anyone other than the polytheist. You have known the disagreement regarding the one in major impurity. As for one in minor impurity: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Muʾayyad billāh, the Hādawiyya, the Chief Judge (Qāḍī al-Quḍāt) and Dāwūd held that it is permissible for him to touch the codex. Al-Qāsim, the majority of jurists, and Imam Yaḥyā said: It is not permissible. They cited what has preceded, and what is in it has preceded. End of al-Shawkānī's words.

**A note on the subtle indication of this verse and what it points to of hidden knowledge:**

The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in *I'lām al-Muwaqqi'īn*, in the discussions on the parables of the Noble Qur'an, something to this effect: What is obligatory regarding that to which the Lawgiver attaches rulings, of words and meanings, is that one should not exceed their words and meanings, nor fall short of them; the word is given its due, and so is the meaning. God, exalted is He, has praised the people of inference (*istinbāṭ*) in His Book, and informed that they are the people of knowledge. It is well known that inference is only the inference of meanings and causes, and the relation of some of them to others; so what is valid among them is considered by the validity of its like, its resemblance, and its counterpart, and what is not valid is discarded. This is what people understand of inference.

Al-Jawhari said: istinbat (deriving, inference) is like istikhraj (extraction). It is known that this is an added measure beyond the mere comprehension of the wording, for that is not the method of istinbat, since the established meanings of words are not attained through istinbat. Rather, through istinbat are attained the causes (ʿilal), the meanings (maʿani), the analogous cases (ashbah) and counterparts (nazaʾir), and the intent of the speaker (maqasid al-mutakallim). God, glorified is He, censured those who heard an apparent meaning in isolation and then spread and publicized it, and He praised those among the people of knowledge (ulu al-ʿilm) who derived (istanbatu) its reality and meaning. What clarifies this is that istinbat is the extraction of a matter which by its nature would be hidden from one other than the one who derives it, and from it is the deriving (istinbat) of water from the land of a well or spring. From this is the saying of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was asked: "Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ single you out with anything apart from the people?" He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul, except for an understanding which Allah grants a servant regarding His Book!" It is known that this understanding is an added measure beyond knowing the established meaning of the wording and its generality or particularity, for that is a shared measure among all who know the Arabic language. Rather, this is the understanding of the implications of the meaning and its counterparts, the intent of the speaker by his speech, and knowing the boundaries of his speech, such that nothing other than what is intended enters into it and nothing of what is intended is excluded from it. When you reflect on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is an honored Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 77] ﴿in a Book well-protected﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 78] ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 79], you will find the verse to be among the clearest proofs of the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ, and that the Qur'an came from Allah, and that the one who brought it is a purified spirit, so the wicked spirits have no path to it. You will also find the verse to be a counterpart to His saying: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 210] ﴿and it is not befitting for them, nor are they able to﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 211], and you will find it indicating in the best indication that none touches the mushaf except one who is pure, and you will find it also indicating in the most subtle indication that none finds its sweetness and taste except one who believes in it and acts by it, as al-Bukhari understood from the verse. He said in his Sahih, in the chapter titled: ﴿Say: Bring the Torah and recite it﴾ [Al ʿImran: 93] ﴿None touches it﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 79] — none finds its taste and benefit except one who believes in the Qur'an, and none carries it in its truth except the believer, in accordance with His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not carry it is like a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 5]. And you will find beneath it also that its meanings are not attained and understood as they should be except by pure hearts, and that impure hearts are prevented from understanding it and turned away from it. So reflect on this near cause, and on the forging of this kinship between these meanings and the apparent meaning of the verse, and on deriving all these meanings from the verse in the best and clearest manner. This is from the understanding to which ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, alluded. End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 56, verses 80–82:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:

[80–82] ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Is it this discourse that you are treating lightly?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81] ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82]

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ means: the One who nurtured them with perfections and guided them to them by sending them down from Himself.

﴿Is it this discourse﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81] means the Qur'an, whose grandeur of status and magnitude of worth have been related to you. ﴿That you are treating lightly?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81] Ibn Jarir said: that is, you soften your speech toward the deniers, colluding with them in denying it and in disbelief. The root of idhhan (ادِّهان, "treating lightly" or "being lax/compromising"), as al-Shihab said, is making a hide or the like "madhhun" (مَدْهُون, anointed) with some oil; since that softens it in a perceptible way, the term was used for the non-material softening, either as a metaphor for softness in general, or it was borrowed for it. For this reason, placating and flattery were called mudahana (مُداهَنة, flattery). This is a well-known metaphor, and because of its fame it became a conventional literal usage; therefore it is also used here metaphorically for laxity, since one who is lax about a matter is not firm in it.

﴿And you make your provision that you deny it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82] means: in return for your provision from Him, you make your thanks to Him the denial of it, disbelieving His blessing and rejecting His favour.

Ibn Jarir said: that is, you make the thanks to God for His provision to you to be denial, and this is like the saying of one person to another: "You made my kindness to you into an injury from you to me"; meaning: you made the thanks for my kindness, or the reward for my kindness to you, into an injury from you to me.

It has been mentioned from al-Haytham ibn Adi that among the dialect of Azd Shanu'ah is the phrase "ma ruziqa fulan" (مَا رُزِقَ فُلانٌ), meaning "what so-and-so did not thank for." End of quotation.

Some have taken the provision here to mean blessing in general, but the more apparent meaning is that it is the blessing of the Qur'an, given the context.

Al-Qashani said: that is, you make your inward nourishment and your true provision the denial of it, because of your veiling yourselves with your own knowledge and your rejection of what is not of its kind, like the rejection of an ignorant man of what contradicts his belief, as if his knowledge were itself a denial of it. Or [it means] your outward provision: because of your constant denial, as if you made denial your nourishment, just as one says to someone persistent in lying: "Lying is his food."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 56, verses 83–85:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[83–85] ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] reaches the throat﴾ ﴿while you are at that moment watching﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 84] ﴿And We are closer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 85]

﴿Then why, when it reaches﴾, i.e., the soul, as the context indicates it, ﴿the throat﴾. ﴿while you are at that moment watching﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 84], i.e., at the time of its extraction, or "you are waiting for the utterance of the last breath." The address is to those around the dying person. ﴿And We are closer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 85]. The majority of the early scholars (al-Salaf) said: it means the Angel of Death is closer to him than his family, but you do not see the angels. Or: you do not perceive the reality of what he is suffering. Some interpreted the nearness as nearness of knowledge and power. The statements have already been expounded upon, and the first view was preferred in the interpretation of the verse: ﴿And We are closer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16] in Surah Qaf, so return to it, for it is important.

This sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah), or it is a circumstantial clause (haliyyah) like the one before it.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 56, verses 86–96:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[86–96] ﴿Then why, if you are not subject to being judged?﴾ ﴿Would you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] (p-5667) ﴿But if he is among those brought near,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88] ﴿then there is rest and sweet provision and a Garden of bliss.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89] ﴿And if he is among the companions of the right,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90] ﴿then "Peace be upon you" from the companions of the right.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91] ﴿But if he is among the deniers, the astray,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92] ﴿then a welcome of boiling water,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 93] ﴿and burning in Hellfire.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94] ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95] ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96]

﴿Then why, if you are not subject to being judged?﴾ That is: not to be recompensed on the Day of Resurrection. Or: not subject to being owned and overpowered. It derives from "dana-hu", meaning he humbled him and enslaved him. ﴿Would you not bring it back﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] means: you would return the soul to its place when it reaches the throat. ﴿if you are truthful﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] means: in your claim that you are not governed, not ruled, and not overpowered.

The meaning is: you are compelled and powerless under the dominion of Lordship. Otherwise you would have been able to repel what you dislike most intensely, which is death. ﴿But if he﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88], that is, the dead person, ﴿is among those brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88], that is, the foremost among the three categories mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

﴿then there is rest﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, for him is ease. ﴿and sweet provision﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, good sustenance, or a flourishing tree whose shade spreads over him. ﴿and a Garden of bliss﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, he enjoys in it what souls desire and what eyes find delightful.

﴿And if he is among the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90], ﴿then "Peace be upon you" from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91]. Ibn Kathir said: that is, the angels give them good tidings of this, saying to one of them: "Peace be upon you," meaning: there is no harm upon you; you are in safety, you are among the companions of the right.

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: he was safe from the punishment of Allah, and the angels of Allah greeted him with peace. As Ikrimah said: the angels greet him and inform him that he is among the companions of the right. This is a good meaning, and it resembles the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat: 30] and the verses that follow. End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: regarding the peace (salam) there are several aspects:

The first: the companion of the right greets the companion of the right with it, as Exalted is He said earlier: ﴿They hear therein no ill speech nor sin,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25] ﴿but only the saying "Peace, peace."﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26]

The second: ﴿Then peace be upon you﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91], that is, safety for you from a matter your heart feared. He is in the highest of ranks. This is like what is said to one whose heart is attached to his absent son, when that son is serving a generous master: "Be free of concern for your son, for he is at rest."

The third: this sentence conveys the greatness of their state, as one says: "So-and-so, enough is he for you," and "It is sufficient for you that he is so-and-so," indicating that he is praised beyond the limit of excellence. End of quotation.

Then al-Razi said: the address in His saying "for you" (laka) may be to the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case there is an aspect to it, which is what we mentioned: that this is consolation for the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ), for they do not need anything of intercession or otherwise. So "peace be upon you, O Muhammad, from them," for they are in safety and well-being; their affair should not trouble you. Or it means: "Peace be upon you, O Muhammad, from them," and that they are among those who greet Muhammad (ﷺ) is a proof of greatness, for the great one is not greeted except by a great one. End of quotation.

﴿But if he is among the deniers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92], that is, of the signs of Allah, ﴿the astray﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92], that is, those who deviate from His path.

﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 93], that is, water whose heat has reached its extreme; this is his drink.

﴿and burning in Hellfire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94], that is, being burned by the fire.

﴿Indeed, this﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95], that is, what has been mentioned of the states of the three groups and their outcomes, ﴿is the certain truth﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95] (p-5669), that is, the reality of the matter and the clear state of affairs, with no confusion or doubt in it. The idafah (genitive construction) here is either an idafah of the described to the descriptor, meaning "the true certainty," as one says "the abode of the Hereafter," or the reverse, meaning "the certainty that is true." Or it is an idafah of the general to the specific, meaning "like the knowledge of the certain matter," in which case the idafah is then of the lam type (meaning "of"), or it has the meaning of min (meaning "from").

Note: In al-Iklil, it is inferred from these verses that the soul, after its separation from the body, is either in bliss or in punishment, and that the abode of the souls of believers is in Paradise, and the souls of disbelievers are in the Fire.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96], that is, declare Him far above what they attribute to Him of falsehoods, and above what they utter of misguidance, in word and in deed.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 56, verses 86–96:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[86–96] ﴿Then why, if you are not subject to being judged?﴾ ﴿Would you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] (p-5667) ﴿But if he is among those brought near,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88] ﴿then there is rest and sweet provision and a Garden of bliss.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89] ﴿And if he is among the companions of the right,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90] ﴿then "Peace be upon you" from the companions of the right.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91] ﴿But if he is among the deniers, the astray,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92] ﴿then a welcome of boiling water,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 93] ﴿and burning in Hellfire.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94] ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95] ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96]

﴿Then why, if you are not subject to being judged?﴾ That is: not to be recompensed on the Day of Resurrection. Or: not subject to being owned and overpowered. It derives from "dana-hu", meaning he humbled him and enslaved him. ﴿Would you not bring it back﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] means: you would return the soul to its place when it reaches the throat. ﴿if you are truthful﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] means: in your claim that you are not governed, not ruled, and not overpowered.

The meaning is: you are compelled and powerless under the dominion of Lordship. Otherwise you would have been able to repel what you dislike most intensely, which is death. ﴿But if he﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88], that is, the dead person, ﴿is among those brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88], that is, the foremost among the three categories mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

﴿then there is rest﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, for him is ease. ﴿and sweet provision﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, good sustenance, or a flourishing tree whose shade spreads over him. ﴿and a Garden of bliss﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, he enjoys in it what souls desire and what eyes find delightful.

﴿And if he is among the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90], ﴿then "Peace be upon you" from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91]. Ibn Kathir said: that is, the angels give them good tidings of this, saying to one of them: "Peace be upon you," meaning: there is no harm upon you; you are in safety, you are among the companions of the right.

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: he was safe from the punishment of Allah, and the angels of Allah greeted him with peace. As Ikrimah said: the angels greet him and inform him that he is among the companions of the right. This is a good meaning, and it resembles the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat: 30] and the verses that follow. End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: regarding the peace (salam) there are several aspects:

The first: the companion of the right greets the companion of the right with it, as Exalted is He said earlier: ﴿They hear therein no ill speech nor sin,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25] ﴿but only the saying "Peace, peace."﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26]

The second: ﴿Then peace be upon you﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91], that is, safety for you from a matter your heart feared. He is in the highest of ranks. This is like what is said to one whose heart is attached to his absent son, when that son is serving a generous master: "Be free of concern for your son, for he is at rest."

The third: this sentence conveys the greatness of their state, as one says: "So-and-so, enough is he for you," and "It is sufficient for you that he is so-and-so," indicating that he is praised beyond the limit of excellence. End of quotation.

Then al-Razi said: the address in His saying "for you" (laka) may be to the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case there is an aspect to it, which is what we mentioned: that this is consolation for the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ), for they do not need anything of intercession or otherwise. So "peace be upon you, O Muhammad, from them," for they are in safety and well-being; their affair should not trouble you. Or it means: "Peace be upon you, O Muhammad, from them," and that they are among those who greet Muhammad (ﷺ) is a proof of greatness, for the great one is not greeted except by a great one. End of quotation.

﴿But if he is among the deniers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92], that is, of the signs of Allah, ﴿the astray﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92], that is, those who deviate from His path.

﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 93], that is, water whose heat has reached its extreme; this is his drink.

﴿and burning in Hellfire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94], that is, being burned by the fire.

﴿Indeed, this﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95], that is, what has been mentioned of the states of the three groups and their outcomes, ﴿is the certain truth﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95] (p-5669), that is, the reality of the matter and the clear state of affairs, with no confusion or doubt in it. The idafah (genitive construction) here is either an idafah of the described to the descriptor, meaning "the true certainty," as one says "the abode of the Hereafter," or the reverse, meaning "the certainty that is true." Or it is an idafah of the general to the specific, meaning "like the knowledge of the certain matter," in which case the idafah is then of the lam type (meaning "of"), or it has the meaning of min (meaning "from").

Note: In al-Iklil, it is inferred from these verses that the soul, after its separation from the body, is either in bliss or in punishment, and that the abode of the souls of believers is in Paradise, and the souls of disbelievers are in the Fire.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96], that is, declare Him far above what they attribute to Him of falsehoods, and above what they utter of misguidance, in word and in deed.

This is like what is said to one whose heart is attached to his absent son, when that son is serving a generous master: "Be free of concern for your son, for he is at rest."

The third: this sentence conveys the greatness of their state, as one says: "So-and-so, enough is he for you," and "It is sufficient for you that he is so-and-so," indicating that he is praised beyond the limit of excellence. End of quotation.

Then al-Razi said: the address in His saying "for you" (laka) may be to the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case there is an aspect to it, which is what we mentioned: that this is consolation for the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ), for they do not need anything of intercession or otherwise. So "peace be upon you, O Muhammad, from them," for they are in safety and well-being; their affair should not trouble you. Or it means: "Peace be upon you, O Muhammad, from them," and that they are among those who greet Muhammad (ﷺ) is a proof of greatness, for the great one is not greeted except by a great one. End of quotation.

﴿But if he is among the deniers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92], that is, of the signs of Allah, ﴿the astray﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92], that is, those who deviate from His path.

﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 93], that is, water whose heat has reached its extreme; this is his drink.

﴿and burning in Hellfire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94], that is, being burned by the fire.

﴿Indeed, this﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95], that is, what has been mentioned of the states of the three groups and their outcomes, ﴿is the certain truth﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95] (p-5669), that is, the reality of the matter and the clear state of affairs, with no confusion or doubt in it. The idafah (genitive construction) here is either an idafah of the described to the descriptor, meaning "the true certainty," as one says "the abode of the Hereafter," or the reverse, meaning "the certainty that is true." Or it is an idafah of the general to the specific, meaning "like the knowledge of the certain matter," in which case the idafah is then of the lam type (meaning "of"), or it has the meaning of min (meaning "from").

Note: In al-Iklil, it is inferred from these verses that the soul, after its separation from the body, is either in bliss or in punishment, and that the abode of the souls of believers is in Paradise, and the souls of disbelievers are in the Fire.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96], that is, declare Him far above what they attribute to Him of falsehoods, and above what they utter of misguidance, in word and in deed.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 56, verses 86–96:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[86–96] ﴿Then why, if you are not subject to being judged?﴾ ﴿Would you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] (p-5667) ﴿But if he is among those brought near,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88] ﴿then there is rest and sweet provision and a Garden of bliss.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89] ﴿And if he is among the companions of the right,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90] ﴿then "Peace be upon you" from the companions of the right.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91] ﴿But if he is among the deniers, the astray,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92] ﴿then a welcome of boiling water,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 93] ﴿and burning in Hellfire.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94] ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95] ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96]

﴿Then why, if you are not subject to being judged?﴾ That is: not to be recompensed on the Day of Resurrection. Or: not subject to being owned and overpowered. It derives from "dana-hu", meaning he humbled him and enslaved him. ﴿Would you not bring it back﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] means: you would return the soul to its place when it reaches the throat. ﴿if you are truthful﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] means: in your claim that you are not governed, not ruled, and not overpowered.

The meaning is: you are compelled and powerless under the dominion of Lordship. Otherwise you would have been able to repel what you dislike most intensely, which is death. ﴿But if he﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88], that is, the dead person, ﴿is among those brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88], that is, the foremost among the three categories mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

﴿then there is rest﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, for him is ease. ﴿and sweet provision﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, good sustenance, or a flourishing tree whose shade spreads over him. ﴿and a Garden of bliss﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89], that is, he enjoys in it what souls desire and what eyes find delightful.

﴿And if he is among the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90], ﴿then "Peace be upon you" from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91]. Ibn Kathir said: that is, the angels give them good tidings of this, saying to one of them: "Peace be upon you," meaning: there is no harm upon you; you are in safety, you are among the companions of the right.

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: he was safe from the punishment of Allah, and the angels of Allah greeted him with peace. As Ikrimah said: the angels greet him and inform him that he is among the companions of the right. This is a good meaning, and it resembles the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat: 30] and the verses that follow.
